message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The pilot is a useful base and most of the cost arithmetic is correct. But the study's three headline conclusions don't hold up against its own figures:

- **Uniform roll-out:** the pilot shows flats participating at about a third of the rate of houses.
- **Local treatment:** Brookfield can take only about 60% of the projected tonnage.
- **Full funding:** with corrected figures, the margin over the provisional allocation disappears, and the net cost probably exceeds it.

## What checks out

- **Table 1 rates:** 2,112 / 3,200 = 66%, 168 / 800 = 21%, 2,280 / 4,000 = 57%. The combined yield rounds to 1.9 kg.
- **Table 2:** 6 × £165,000 / 7 = £141,400 and 12 × £34,000 = £408,000. The total of £733,400 is correct.
- **The projection's arithmetic:** 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 = 3,290 t, as stated. The disposal saving of 3,290 × £74 = £243,000 is also correct.

## Major issues

**1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types.**
Houses participated at **66%**, flats at **21%**, about one-third the rate. Flats also produced less per participating household (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg). The pilot is clear evidence that flats need a different approach, such as communal bins at bin stores, liners delivered to the door, or targeted engagement. It is not evidence for a single uniform service.

**2. The projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot.**
Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but the pilot's overall rate was **57%**. The pilot's mix (20% flats) matches the district's, so its figures can be scaled directly by housing type:

| | Households | Rate | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

The projection is overstated by about 420 tonnes (13%). The disposal saving falls from £243,000 to about **£213,000**.

**3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage.**
Brookfield offers **1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. Even the corrected projection is about 2,870 tonnes. That leaves roughly **1,070 tonnes a year** with no treatment route in the study, for at least two years. The only alternative named is 46 miles away. Its gate fee and the extra haulage costs aren't given, and they could absorb most or all of the £74 saving on those tonnes.

At Brookfield alone, the saving is 1,800 × £74 = **£133,000**. The author's statement that "treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the food waste.

**4. "Fully funded" rests on a thin margin that has already gone.**

| | Net annual cost |
|---|---|
| As stated | £490,000 |
| Corrected tonnage | ~£520,000 |
| Corrected tonnage, overflow saving nothing | ~£600,000 |
| **Provisional allocation** | **£520,000** |

The £520,000 is also **provisional**, not confirmed.

**5. "Every cost line is shown" isn't the case.**
Likely omissions:
- **Staff on-costs.** If £34,000 is salary, employer NI and pension typically add 25–30%, around £100,000–£120,000 a year.
- **Relief cover** for holidays and sickness, and **supervision**.
- **A spare vehicle.** Six vehicles for six rounds leaves no cover for breakdowns or servicing.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in section 6.
- **Haulage and gate fees** for the overflow tonnage.
- **Ongoing liner supply** after the initial three months, unless the £88,000 covers it. The study should say.
- **Upfront capital.** About £990,000 for vehicles, plus caddies, is needed before April 2027, whatever the annualised figures.

## Other points

- **Statutory deadline.** My understanding is that the Simpler Recycling rules required English councils to start weekly food waste collections by **31 March 2026**, with transitional arrangements for some councils. Please check this against current guidance. If Thornbury has no transitional arrangement, an April 2027 start is already late. Section 1 should state the legal deadline and Thornbury's position.
- **The timetable has no slack.** The vehicles take three months from order to delivery, and crews are trained the month before launch. A late delivery delays the start, and there's no contingency plan.
- **The pilot may overstate long-run participation.** Six months is short; participation often falls after the novelty wears off, and January–June may not reflect year-round food waste.
- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households." Without a response rate, it may mostly reflect participants, who are likely to be the most positive.

## On the author's description

- **"Participation held up across houses and flats"** is contradicted by Table 1 (66% against 21%).
- **"Consistent yields"** isn't quite right: 1.9 kg against 1.4 kg.
- **"Every cost line is shown"** misses on-costs, relief, a spare vehicle, overflow treatment and the phone line.
- **"Treatment is local"** holds for about 1,800 of roughly 2,870 tonnes.
- **"Fully funded"** depends on a provisional allocation and goes from a small surplus to a probable deficit once the figures are corrected.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Replace the uniform-service conclusion** with a separate approach for flats, using the pilot's own figures to justify it.
2. **Re-project tonnage by housing type** (about 2,870 t), and include a scenario with lower long-run participation.
3. **Secure treatment for the full tonnage** until 2029, and cost the overflow route.
4. **Complete the costing:** on-costs, relief, supervision, a spare vehicle, the phone line, liners and overflow haulage. Show capital costs separately.
5. **Present funding as a range** against the provisional allocation, and state what happens if the confirmed figure is lower.
6. **State the statutory deadline** and Thornbury's compliance position.

Approving the vehicle order may still be the right decision, especially if the service is legally overdue. But Cabinet should approve it knowing the service is likely to cost more than the funding currently covers, and that it needs a second treatment route and a separate plan for flats.
